LLM auditresponse for unreal-engine-5-pacman-cache.hook:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This file is a standard pacman hook that runs `paccache` after installing or upgrading the `unreal-engine` package. `paccache` is a tool from the `pacman-contrib` package used to manage the package cache. The command `/usr/bin/paccache -rvk1 unreal-engine` removes all but the most recent cached version of the package (`-k1` keeps one version). This is a common and expected practice to save storage space. There is no obfuscation, network activity, or any other malicious behavior. The hook does nothing beyond its stated purpose.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>
<summary>Standard pacman hook to clean cache, no security issues.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for unreal-engine.install:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This `.install` script is a standard post-installation hook for an Arch Linux package. It creates a system group `unreal`, ensures the engine installation directory is group-owned by that group, and removes the group on package removal. All operations are confined to legitimate system administration tasks: reading a local config file (`/usr/share/unreal-engine/install-prefix`), creating/deleting a group, and changing file ownership. There are no network requests, obfuscated code, execution of fetched content, or manipulation of data outside the package's own scope. The script follows normal packaging practices for multi-user applications that require group-based permissions.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>
<summary>Standard group ownership management; no malicious behavior.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD follows standard AUR packaging practices for Unreal Engine. It clones the official upstream source, applies patches, runs the engine's own Setup.sh and BuildGraph scripts, and installs the compiled output. There are no hidden network requests to unknown hosts, no obfuscated code, and no attempts to exfiltrate data or execute untrusted payloads.

The only external fetch outside the engine's own domains is an optional alternative desktop icon downloaded from `raw.githubusercontent.com/EliverLara/candy-icons`. This is a static SVG file (not code) and the download is gated by a user-configurable flag. While fetching from a mutable branch is a hygiene concern, it does not execute the downloaded content and is not evidence of a supply-chain attack. All other sources are pinned with sha256 checksums or come from the official Epic Games repository.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>
<summary>Legitimate Unreal Engine package with no malicious code.</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The script is a straightforward launcher for Unreal Engine 5. It performs routine setup tasks: verifying the user is not root, creating Steam-related symlinks and required directories (including a typo directory `~/.cnfig/` which appears to be a harmless mistake), copying a desktop file to the user's local applications, and launching the editor. The checksum and path placeholders are intended to be replaced during packaging and pose no risk in themselves. There are no network requests, no execution of fetched code, no obfuscation, and no attempts to exfiltrate or tamper with system files. All operations are confined to the user's home directory and standard application paths, consistent with normal packaging behavior.
</details>
<evidence>
